analytic.title: EGPS: A Class of Real-Time Scheduling Algorithms Based on Processor Sharing

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: A class of real-time scheduling algorithms EGPS is proposed. Using EGPS, the schedulability of each process is enforced by a guaranteed CPU service rate, independent of the demands of other processes. Our research uses a GPS-based framework for periodic and sporadic process scheduling, jitter control, service rate adjustment, and mixed scheduling of soft and hard real-time processes. We then study the performance of the proposed algorithms by using a generic avionics platform example and a series of simulation experiments in jitter control and mixed scheduling of soft and hard real-time processes.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The real-time resource allocation problem has been an active research topic in the past decades. Optimal scheduling algorithms such as the rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) algorithm, the earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm, and the least slack first (LSF) algorithm [9,10] were proposed in different contexts. In particular, Liu and Layland [9] introduced the concept of achievable utilization factor to provide a quick test for deciding the schedulability of a set of independent periodic processes.

This paper proposes a class of real-time scheduling algorithms based on the idea of generalized processor sharing (GPS) which was suggested by Parekh and Gallager [12] in the context of rate-based flow and congestion control at network gateway nodes. Distinct from the past work, e.g., [6,9,10,11], the schedulability of each process in GPS-based systems is guaranteed with an assigned CPU service rate, independent of the demands of other Supported in part by a research grant from the National Science Council under Grants NSC85-2213-E-194-008 and NSC87-2213-E-194-002 processes. In this paper, we propose an optimal dynamic scheduling algorithm called Earliest-Completion-Time GPS (EGPS) and extensions for jitter-control, service rate adjustment, and sporadic process scheduling. The response time of each sporadic process can be guaranteed either statically or stochastically. We develop the theoretical foundation to assign proper CPU service rates to processes to improve the schedulability of the whole system and demonstrate the feasibility of the rate adjustment mechanism by a case study on the generic avionics platform example [8]. Our experimental results also show that the EGPS algorithms have good performances in mixing the scheduling of soft and hard realtime processes and in largely reducing process jitters.

The contribution of this work is as follows: (1) A generic GPS-based scheduling framework is proposed for periodic and sporadic process scheduling. (2) A rate adjustment mechanism has been deveopled to meet the response time requirement of each individual periodic or sporadic process.
(3) The idea of CPU bandwidth preservation is used successfully in jitter control and mixed scheduling of hard and soft real-time processes.

The rest of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 summarizes the related research. Section 3 shows how to model a process set as a collection of traffic sessions for GPS-based process scheduling. Section 4 presents the basic EGPS algorithm which simulates the GPS algorithm without the impractical assumptions of GPS algorithm. We then extend the EGPS algorithm to provide jitter-control, completion time adjustment, and sporadic process scheduling in Section 5. Section 6 presents a case study and experimental results using the proposed algorithms. The paper is concluded in Section 7.

div.head: Related Work
div.p: Recently the idea of generalized processor sharing (GPS) has received a great deal of attention in the context of process scheduling and packet transmission [3,4,12,16,17,18,19]. Parekh and Gallager [12] were the first to use the idea of GPS for rate-based flow and congestion control at network gateway nodes. Waldspurger and Weihl [18,19] were the first to develop a process scheduling algorithm based on the idea of GPS. Their algorithm allocates a time quantum to the process which has the worst progress in the system according to its resource reservation. They showed that the service time lag of a process at any time can be reduced to Olog n, the service time lag being the difference between the service time that a process should receive under GPS, and the time it actually receives. Stoica, et al. [17] proposed and analyzed another GPS-based process scheduling algorithm, where CPU time is allocated in discrete-sized time quanta such that a process, regardless of whether it is a real-time or non-real-time process, makes progress at a uniform rate. They were the first to implement and to test a GPS-based process scheduling algorithm which guarantees constant lag bounds. Sprui, et al. [16] proposed an effective mechansim called TB server to service sporadic processes. The capacity and performance of a TB server is guaranteed by preserving the CPU bandwidth. The schedulability of a TB server and other processes in the system is guaranteed under the framework of the EDF scheduling. A rejection mechanism is also proposed for overload handling of a TB server. Deng, et al. [3,4] proposed a two-level hierarchical scheme for scheduling real-time and non-real-time (multi-threaded) applications. The schedulability of each application is guaranteed independently from other applications by an underlying OS scheduler which adopts the idea of GPS. Within each application, different scheduling algorithms might be used. They considered different contexts such as the existence of global resource sharing and non-preemptable critical sections among applications.

Our proposed scheduling algorithm EGPS is closely related to the process scheduling algorithms proposed in [3,4,16,17,18,19]. The advanced techniques from the above-mentioned work, such as lag management, quantumbased scheduling, TB server, and two-level hierarchical scheduling scheme, are orthogonal to our work and can be made to complement each other. For example, each TB server or real-time application can be considered as a periodic (or sporadic) process in the EGPS algorithms. Various techniques, such as service rate adjustment, developed in this paper can be applied to the performance and/or capacity management of TB servers or real-time applications in an open environment [3,4,16].

div.head: GPS-Based Scheduling
div.p: We first review the Generalized Processor Sharing (GPS) algorithm for scheduling an independent periodic process set and show that the GPS algorithm is an optimal scheduling algorithm with the achievable utilization factor equal to 100.

GPS is a scheduling algorithm based on the concept of the reservation ratio of processor computation time. Suppose a GPS server executes at a fixed rate r, and each traffic session i is characterized by a positive real number i , i = 1 ; 2; ; N ( i is called the reservation ratio of session i). When combined with leaky bucket admission control, the worst-case performance on throughput and delay can be guaranteed. GPS is a work-conserving algorithm. However, GPS is an idealized multiplexing discipline for packet transmission since it assumes that the traffic is infinitely divisible such that the server can serve multiple traffic sessions simultaneously.

We now show how to model a process set as a collection of traffic sessions for GPS-based process scheduling. Let c i and p i be the computation time and period of a periodic process i , respectively, for i = 1 ; 2; ; N . Each process i is modeled as a traffic session i in which a packet of size c i arrives at a regular interval p i , and i equal to the utilization factor u i = ci pi .

div.head: Earliest-Completion-time GPS (EGPS) Scheduling
div.p: Although GPS may schedule any process set with a 100 utilization, it assumes that processes are infinitely divisible such that the server can serve them virtually simultaneously. Therefore, the GPS algorithm is impractical for actual computer systems. The Earliest-Completion-Time GPS (EGPS) scheduling algorithm is designed to simulate the GPS algorithm with much lower run-time overheads.

div.head: The EGPS Protocol
div.p: As in GPS, each process i is modeled as a traffic session i in which a packet of size c i arrives at a regular interval p i .

The GPS completion time of a process request is the time at which the corresponding packet will be transmitted under the GPS algorithm. The reservation ratio i of process i is set to its utilization factor u i = ci pi .

div.head: The EGPS algorithm:
div.p: EGPS uses a preemptive priority-driven scheduling approach in which processes are scheduled in the order of their GPS completion times. Any ready process request with the earliest GPS completion time is executed first. Processes with the same GPS completion time are executed on a FCFS basis. 2

The GPS completion time for each process is computed based on the total load at the time. Since the total system load changes with the arrival or the completion of every process request, all GPS completion times must be updated accordingly. Therefore, the implementation of EGPS depends on the existence of an efficient way to track the system load.

Our proposed mechanism is based on the idea of virtual time [12]. Define each arrival or departure, i.e., service completion, of a packet from the GPS server as an event, and t i the real time at which the i th event occurs. B i is the set of process requests that are ready for execution in the interval t i,1 ; t i . Virtual time V t is defined to be zero for all times when the server is idle. div.head: Extensions: Jitter Control, Rate Adjustment, and Sporadic Process Scheduling
div.p: Using EGPS, the reservation ratio i of each process i is set to its utilization factor u i = ci pi . Processes are also assumed to be periodic. In this section, we present some extensions of the EGPS algorithm: (1) The ready time of a process in each period may be adjusted to minimize the variation of the completion times of a process in consecutive periods. (2) The reservation ratio i of each process i may be different from its utilization factor u i to allow the adjustment of the response time of process i . (3) The re- sponse time of each sporadic process is considered in the same framework for scheduling periodic processes.

div.head: Jitter-Control EGPS (JEGPS)
div.p: In some real-time applications, the temporal distance between consecutive completions of a process must be controlled to reduce the jitters. When a process produces the result too late in a period, it is better not to produce the result too early in the next period. div.head: Performance Evaluation
div.p: The performance of the proposed algorithms was verified by a case study on the generic avionics platform example [8] and a series of simulation experiments. A number of simulations experiments were done to compare the performance of the EGPS algorithms (EGPS and JEGPS) with other well-known real-time scheduling algorithms such as the rate monotonic scheduling (RMS) algorithm, the earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm, the least slack first (LSF) algorithm, and the first-in-first-out (FIFO) algorithm. The LSF algorithm used a fixed slack (equal to the period minus the computation time) for each process.

The primary performance metrics used in this paper are the jitter of process executions in consecutive periods, referred to as the Jitter, and the ratio of requests that miss deadlines, referred to as the Miss Ratio. div.head: Jitter Control and Scheduling of Mixed Process Sets
div.p: We now study the capability of the EGPS algorithm in jitter control of processes scheduled in a uniprocessor environment and in mixed scheduling of hard and soft real-time processes. Process sets in the simulation experiments were generated by a random number generator. The number of processes in a process set ranged from 10 to 20. The utilization factor of a process ranged from 2 to 30, and the period of a process ranged from 10 to 1000. Ten process sets were simulated for each system utilization factor, and the simulation results were averaged. Each process set was simulated for all scheduling algorithms from time 0 to time 2; 000; 000. When mixed scheduling of hard and soft realtime processes is considered, the ratio of the total utilization factors of hard real-time and soft real-time processes is 1 : 2 . Figure 3 shows that JEGPS greatly outperforms EDF, RMS, FIFO, LSF, and EGPS in reducing the jitters of processes in a uniprocessor environment. The lower the system utilization factor, the better the jitter control for JEGPS because of more flexibility in adjusting the ready time of processes.

Figure 4 shows that the miss ratio of hard real-time processes scheduled by EDF, RMS, FIFO, LSF, and EGPS, re- spectively. EGPS greatly outperforms other scheduling algorithms, and the schedulability of hard real-time processes was fully guaranteed. It is also interesting to see that the miss ratio of soft real-time processes scheduled by EGPS is very low, as shown in Figure 5. The low miss ratio of soft real-time processes scheduled by EGPS is partially because the EGPS reservation ratio for the processor was given to soft real-time processes in inverse order of their periods in the experiments.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: This paper proposes a class of optimal real-time scheduling algorithms based on the idea of generalized processor sharing. The schedulability of each process is guaranteed by an assigned CPU service rate, independent of the demands of other processes. We have presented a GPSbased scheduling framework for periodic and sporadic process scheduling, jitter control, service rate adjustment, and mixed scheduling of soft and hard real-time processes. The strength of the proposed algorithms is verified by a case study on the generic avionics example [8].

Past research on process scheduling, e.g., [9,10], has concentrated on the schedulability problem or the feasibility problem of a process system. Researchers proposed various "optimal" scheduling algorithms with a good achievable utilization factor but ignored properties such as jitter management which may be important to some commercial time-critical systems such as Video-on-Demand systems [7]. We believe that more research in exploiting the application semantics and the needs of application systems may provide the best reward in solving the resource allocation problem. For future research, we will extend the EGPS algorithms to distributed real-time systems. With the homogenity of the EGPS algorithms and network scheduling algorithms such as the Packet-by-Packet GPS algorithm [12], we expect that the EGPS algorithms will be better in handling processes with end-to-end delay requirements in a distributed real-time system [5,6,11].
